item.title: 'Lawyer up': Democrats prepare to investigate Trump after taking Congress
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) speaks with reporters during an election night watch party in Washington on Nov. 3, 2026. (Tom Brenner / Getty Images) Democrats in Congress gained the power Tuesday night to more forcefully investigate President Trump and rein in his agenda, setting up confrontations that are likely to define the final two years of his presidency. As party leaders on Wednesday celebrated retaking the House and Senate, they vowed to put Trump and his administration on the defensive with subpoenas and hearings, a role that voters made clear they want them to play . But they also said the top priority would be the issue that swept them to power: making life more affordable. “We are going to work hard to drive costs down with the president or without him, period,” Sen. Chuck Schumer, who is poised to become Senate majority leader, said at a news conference. Schumer’s fellow New Yorker and the House Democratic leader, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, echoed those priorities on CNN: “We ran on affordability, we won decisively on affordability, and now we have a responsibility to govern on affordability.” With power split between the legislative and executive branches, to what degree Washington avoids gridlock will depend on how Trump wields his veto pen and how the Democrats negotiate with him — and how they follow through on pledges to investigate what they called a corrupt administration. “Make no mistake, whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court and entangle him in legislative razor wire,” Schumer said. “The days of Trump’s supplicant Senate are over.” Read more: Democrats' historic rout was fueled by massive voter swing to the left Trump, for his part, congratulated Democrats, but on Fox News said, “They are in control, but they’re really not in control. They can send over 50 different, great bills that they’re all excited about, and I send them back with a nice stamp veto.” Trump added that he has “friends” in the Democratic Party and is willing to make deals. “I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything,” he said. Schumer argued that the Democrats’ decisive victories show the president’s weakness and give them legislative leverage, and he warned Republicans against resisting their agenda. “If they continue to embrace Trump, they are going to be following him right over the cliff, as this election has shown, and it will get even worse for them,” he said. After four years out of power, House Democrats plan to carry out plans they have spent months mapping out — investigating the Trump family’s business dealings, allegedly corrupt deals by administration officials and suspected abuses by federal immigration agents. In a sign of what is to come, Rep. Robert Garcia of Long Beach, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, wrote on X: “LAWYER UP.” Read more: 'Not a hit on me': Trump faults candidates and Fox News, not himself, for Republican losses Democrats also intend to summon top Cabinet officials to testify on many hot-button issues, such as the war in Iran. They could also bring oil, insurance, pharmaceutical and other industries under congressional scrutiny. That oversight tactic could help Democrats’ push to lower costs regardless of whether they can get Trump to sign legislation. The Democrat majorities in both chambers are substantial. In the Senate, where Republicans held a 53-47 majority going into Tuesday, Democrats have won 54 seats to Republicans’ 44 as of Wednesday, according to Associated Press projections. In the House, Republicans entered the election with 218 seats to Democrats’ 214. Now, Democrats have 237 seats, well past the 218 needed for a majority, and some races remain undecided. The Senate majority hands Democrats the ability to block Trump’s judicial and other nominations — including appointments to the Supreme Court. Democrats do not have the numbers, however, to reach the two-thirds majority needed to override Trump’s veto. The Democratic victory will also probably kick off a new chapter of the party’s tug-of-war over its identity. A group of insurgent progressives, several of them democratic socialists who defeated establishment-backed candidates in primaries, will join a caucus whose majority includes moderates from Republican-leaning districts. Read more: Fears of election day interference fizzle, but federal war on voter fraud could continue Holding together a caucus that stretches from democratic socialists to centrists is likely to be the first major test for Jeffries, who is poised to become speaker. Much of that balancing act could run through California, more than any other state. Its Democrats form the largest bloc in the new majority, and several are in line for powerful posts. Among them is Garcia, who is in line to lead the Oversight Committee and vowed last month to investigate possible corruption by the Trump family and administration officials. The committee, Garcia said, will also “focus on issues around the survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and on corporate corruption. But our fourth major investigative area is going to be on the abuses of ICE and DHS.” Garcia said that the committee has flagged more than 1,000 instances of “credible, verifiable abuses by federal immigration agents,” and that scrutinizing those examples will be a key part of the panel’s work in the coming months. He added that he also would like to look into white nationalist groups’ role in recruiting federal immigration agents. As Democrats lay the groundwork for investigations, many in the party are wary of the most aggressive tool available to them: impeachment. Trump, the only president to have been impeached twice, has said it would be “very unfair” if Democrats move to impeach him a third time. Some Democrats have floated impeachment as an option, but others argue it could distract from their affordability agenda. Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, which plays a key role in the impeachment process, told MS NOW in August that Trump is “very eager” for Democrats to impeach him so he can mobilize his political base. “We’re not going to play into the game,” he said. Get the L.A. Times California Politics newsletter. Deeply reported insights into legislation, politics and policy from Sacramento, Washington and beyond, in your inbox twice per week. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . This article originally appeared on LA Times at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/lawyer-democrats-seize-congress-plot-195645078.html

item.title: Trump dismisses possibility of replacing Hegseth amid Iran war fallout
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump said Wednesday that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth would remain on the job, even as he acknowledged that the war with Iran had contributed to Republicans' sweeping midterm losses and as Democrats prepare to use their new congressional majority to potentially investigate the Pentagon chief. Trump dismissed the possibility of replacing Hegseth, telling reporters he was "doing a great job." When asked about speculation that Hegseth is eyeing Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn's soon-to-be-vacated Tennessee seat, Trump predicted the defense secretary would be "very popular" in the state. Blackburn, who won Tennessee's gubernatorial race Tuesday, declined to weigh in on who might be picked to fill her Senate seat. Asked about who would be appointed, she said, "It's not a conversation for today." Hegseth says War Powers deadline doesn't apply because of ceasefire with Iran Trump's remarks come as Republicans grapple with the political fallout from the eight-month war with Iran, which has driven up gas prices and fueled voter frustration over the cost of living. The war and its economic consequences are widely seen as a major factor in Republicans' crushing midterm defeat. "The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it," Trump told reporters, adding that he believes the war will be worth it in the long term. In April, Hegseth declared a "historic and overwhelming victory" over Iran. But fighting has continued for months, killing and wounding American troops, driving up energy costs and consuming expensive U.S. munitions that could take years to replace. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images - PHOTO: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks while participating in a discussion during the U.S. Army's 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition, October 14, 2026 in Washington. Hegseth intends to remain at the Pentagon through the end of Trump's term, according to his spokesperson. "Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists," Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell told ABC News Wednesday, adding Hegseth is "100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump's term in office." Trump has privately sought input from Republicans close to the White House about how they feel Hegseth is doing in the job, according to sources familiar with the situation, as the administration grapples with the political consequences of the war and the election. Ezra Acayan/Pool via Reuters - PHOTO: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth arrives for the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting, October 28, 2026 in Cebu, Philippines. Democrats say they are preparing to use their new congressional majority to scrutinize an administration that has faced limited oversight during the past two years, with Hegseth expected to be a major target for scrutiny and possible impeachment. Democrats could use their subpoena power to attempt to question Pentagon officials about the Iran war, the legality of strikes on suspected drug-smuggling boats and Hegseth's unexplained firings of senior military officers. But party leaders are also looking to keep affordability at the forefront of their agenda, balancing investigations into the Trump administration with the economic concerns that helped deliver their sweeping midterm wins. Top general fired from Pentagon Joint Staff position for allegedly leaking classified info, source says Vice President JD Vance, who has been widely viewed as a possible contender for the Republican presidential nomination in 2028, distanced himself from the conflict in a candid rebuke of the administration, placing the GOP defeat on the war with Iran. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance said in a social media post Wednesday. "The president himself said so last night." Nationally, 34% of U.S. House voters said that the war in Iran was "crucial" to their vote, while 49% said the same about the cost of living and 55% said government corruption was crucial to their vote, according to ABC News Voter Poll data. Vance argued that Republicans could defend the decision to go to war, but should not ignore the electoral consequences. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," he added. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there." This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-dismisses-prospect-replacing-hegseth-amid-iran-war/story?id=137852219

item.title: Ballot measure results bring new abortion protections and transgender restrictions
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The battle for control of Congress got the lion's share of the attention on Tuesday, but there were a lot of other consequential measures on the ballots that could have a direct impact on voters' lives. Ballot measures often don't receive much national focus, but every two years, voters across the country decide whether to adopt policies that have major implications for their states. This year was no different. There were more than 140 measures on the ballot across 40 states. Many touched on some of the biggest issues in U.S. politics, including abortion, transgender rights, voting and the democratic process itself. Ballot measures can give the people a way to directly alter the laws in their states instead of relying solely on their elected representatives to create policy on their behalf. In some cases, they provide an opportunity for voters to endorse or reject something their state legislature wants to do. In others, regular citizens can get their preferred policy on the ballot directly through a signature-gathering campaign. Here's a rundown of the results of some of the major measures on statewide ballots this year. Abortion The Supreme Court's 2022 decision to overturn the nationwide abortion protections established by Roe v. Wade instantly turned abortion access into a state-by-state issue. It also led to a flurry of ballot measures across the country in which voters were asked to decide whether their states should protect or restrict abortion rights. In the years since, voters have generally come down in favor of protecting abortion rights. That trend got another test this year due to abortion-related measures in four states. In Idaho, voters rejected a measure that would have overturned their state's strict abortion restrictions and established a right to reproductive freedom and privacy, including abortion until fetal viability. The initiative’s failure means Idaho will not join the ranks of red states where voters used ballot measures to expand abortion rights. One of those red states is Missouri , where voters approved a measure in 2024 that struck down some of the nation's most restrictive abortion laws. On Tuesday, voters rejected a Republican-backed measure that would have repealed that 2024 amendment and allowed strict abortion restrictions to be put back into place. That same failed measure would also have created new limits on gender-affirming care in the state. Voters in two other states that already have relatively permissive laws around abortion access — Nevada and Virginia — approved measures that will enshrine abortion rights in their state constitutions, a step that will make it much harder to restrict access in the future. Transgender policy The debate over transgender rights, particularly when it comes to minors, has become a central issue in American politics. It should be no surprise, then, that a number of states had measures related to the topic on the ballot this year. All of them would impose new limits on transgender rights. Four states — Washington, Nebraska, Arizona and Colorado — voted on measures that would ban trans athletes from participating on sports teams that match their gender identity. There are some important differences from state to state, though. The proposals in Washington and Nebraska would only apply to girls' and women's teams. Colorado's and Arizona's would apply to both male and female teams. Washington's bill also includes a stipulation that would require all K-12 students who want to play girls' or women's sports — whether they identify as trans or not — to have their sex verified by a doctor . Arizona's measure will also ban schools from allowing trans minors or adults to access bathrooms, locker rooms or other private spaces designated for a sex that doesn't match the one they were assigned at birth. A separate initiative in Colorado would ban gender-affirming surgeries for minors. The initiatives in Arizona and Nebraska were both approved. Washington’s measure and the two initiatives in Colorado appeared to be on the path to passing as well. The only state where potential new restrictions on transgender rights failed was Missouri, where the new limits were combined with a proposal to repeal abortion rights in the state. Voter ID Six states voted on measures related to voter ID. California and Colorado rejected proposals that would have established or expanded requirements for voters to show ID when they cast their ballots or when voting by mail. A similar measure in Nevada was approved. Arizona, Ohio and North Carolina, where strict voter ID requirements are already in place under state law, considered measures that add or expand those requirements in their state constitutions. Arizona’s failed . The measures in Ohio and North Carolina were approved Schools Schools have been a major flashpoint for culture war battles in recent years. A handful of measures on the ballot Tuesday asked voters to weigh in on some of those debates. Voters in Arizona and Wisconsin both considered proposals to ban affirmative action in schools and all other government agencies. Arizona’s measure failed . Wisconsin’s was approved . Fuse via Getty Images Alabama voters approved a pair of school proposals. One will require public schools to play the national anthem at least once a week. The other will make the recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance a daily requirement and mandate that school boards adopt policies to allow student-led prayer. It’s still too early to know the fate of a sweeping parental rights initiative in Washington that would give parents of public school students substantially more oversight over the education their children receive, including the power to review curricula and textbooks, put strict new limits on the kinds of medical care schools can provide without parental notification and roll back changes to the state's parental rights law that protected against discrimination and bullying in schools. The ballot initiative process Ballot measures frequently center on contentious political issues, but in recent years, the initiative process itself has increasingly become the subject of political debate. Five states voted on measures that would have made it harder for citizen-led ballot initiatives to become law, either by raising the share of the vote certain measures need to get approved or restricting the subjects that initiatives can address. Four of those measures failed. The fifth appears to be on track to also being rejected. Voters in North Dakota and South Dakota shot down measures that would have required any attempt to change their state constitutions to get 60% of the vote. A similar proposal in Utah that would have applied only to tax-related initiatives also failed. A California measure that would also raise the threshold for certain tax-related initiatives was trailing with more than half of the vote counted as of Wednesday afternoon. Changing the threshold for success by 10 percentage points may not sound like a huge deal, but it is often the difference between a proposal becoming law and being rejected. For example, initiatives in Florida that would have legalized abortion and recreational marijuana use both received majority support from voters in 2024, but neither became law because they fell short of the state's 60% approval standard. Voters cast their ballots at a polling location inside the Candia Youth Athletic Association during a primary election in Candia, N.H. Mel Musto/Bloomberg via Getty Images Idaho also rejected a measure that would have banned initiatives aimed at legalizing marijuana, psychedelics and other narcotics. Two states voted to protect the initiative process, as well. Montana voters approved a proposal to amend the state's constitution to guarantee citizens' rights to pursue ballot initiatives and make it harder for the government to interfere with measures approved by voters. In Missouri , voters approved a measure that will prohibit the state's Republican-led legislature from weakening the initiative process. It will also bar it from amending or repealing any measures that have passed unless 80% of both chambers agree to put the change before voters. Other notable initiatives Voters across the country also weighed in on a long list of other pivotal ballot measures that don’t fit neatly into a specific category. Here are a few of them. Arizona voted to ban new traffic cameras without direct voter approval. Nebraska rejected a proposal to legalize online sports betting . Vermont voters overwhelmingly approved a measure to ban discrimination based on gender identity. Virginia voted to restore the voting rights of people convicted of felonies once they're released from prison. A measure in Wisconsin aimed at prohibiting the government from closing places of worship during public health emergencies was rejected. Massachusetts voters chose not to make recreational marijuana sales illegal. Lower-stakes — but still noteworthy — measures included a failed Colorado initiative that would have enshrined the right to hunt and fish in the state constitution and a request for Idaho voters to select an official state gun — they chose the Winchester Model 1873 rifle. This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/article/abortion-transgender-rights-and-voter-id-ballot-measure-results-from-the-2026-midterms-191855364.html

item.title: Supreme Court succession stakes rise after Democrats win control of the Senate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By John Kruzel WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The US midterm election landslide that gives Democrats control of Congress starting in January is fueling questions about the longevity of the Supreme Court's two eldest justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, and the durability of its conservative majority. As Republicans prepare to cede control of the Senate to Democrats for the next two years or ‌more, some conservative commentators already are expressing concerns about the health prospects of Thomas, 78, and Alito, 76, placing renewed focus on their continued service on the top US judicial body. The US Constitution ‌assigns the Senate the power to confirm a president's judicial nominations. With a Senate majority, Democrats can block any nominations that Republican President Donald Trump would make to fill potential Supreme Court vacancies, just as Republicans blocked Democratic President Barack Obama from filling one in ​2016. Thomas has given no public indication of wanting to step down. Alito said last month he would remain for the duration of the current nine-month term, which began in October, even if Democrats were to retake the Senate. Thomas and Alito did not immediately respond to questions from Reuters about whether they are considering retiring. Thomas and Alito are the court's two most conservative justices and have reliably backed Trump policies in major rulings during his second term in office. The court's 6-3 conservative majority, which has steered American law in a sharply rightward direction on issues from abortion to gun rights to presidential powers, includes three justices Trump appointed during his first term as president. Alito's comment about remaining ‌through the current term followed speculation that he might quickly retire in the ⁠event Democrats captured the Senate in order to ensure that Trump could get a successor confirmed with Republicans still in control. Until Democrats formally take over Congress on January 3, the current Republican majority retains control during what is called a lame-duck session. While some conservatives might want Thomas or Alito to retire right away so Trump can nominate a ⁠replacement and a Republican-led Senate could quickly provide confirmation, the tight timeline and other legislative priorities could make that difficult even if the justices had any interest in doing so. 'NAKEDLY POLITICAL' To some legal analysts, the notion of an imminent Supreme Court departure seemed far-fetched. Although justices mulling retirement often consider the politics of the president and party control of the Senate in making a decision, "they do not like to broadcast that they do so," Cornell Law School professor Michael Dorf said. "Absent an acute ​health ​crisis," Dorf said, "a decision to retire in the next several months would appear, and would in fact be, so nakedly political ​that I doubt Justice Alito or Thomas would take it." Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, a ‌prominent Republican who mounted an unsuccessful presidential campaign in 2024, wrote on social media: "Chance of confirming a worthy successor to Justice Thomas and/or Alito during President Trump's term: Zero." The size of the new Democratic majority in the Senate could make it difficult for Republicans to reclaim the chamber in the 2028 elections, according to some analysts, meaning Republicans may not control both the presidency and Senate for quite some time. "If a Republican is elected president in 2028, that president will not be able to appoint any justices or judges until Republicans regain the Senate," said legal analyst Ed Whelan of the Ethics and Public Policy Center, who served as a Justice Department official under Republican President George W. Bush. "Given the deep hole, that might not happen until 2033," Whelan said. Thomas would be 84 and Alito 82 in 2033 when a new Congress is sworn in. That would place them over ‌the average retirement age of around 80 for Supreme Court justices since 2000. 'ON THEIR TREADMILLS' Thomas and Alito have no serious health ​concerns that are publicly known, though each was briefly hospitalized in recent years. Alito was treated for dehydration in March after feeling ​ill during an event in Philadelphia. Thomas missed arguments in cases in 2022 when he was hospitalized ​with flu-like symptoms. Three justices have died in office this century. Conservative Chief Justice William Rehnquist died in 2005 at age 80. Conservative Justice Antonin Scalia died in 2016 at ‌79. Liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg died in 2020 at 87. A Republican-led Senate refused ​to consider Obama's nominee to replace Scalia, allowing Trump the ​following year to fill the vacancy. The Senate confirmed Trump's nominee Amy Coney Barrett swiftly in the weeks after Ginsburg's death to build the court's current 6-3 conservative edge. Ginsburg's decision not to retire during Obama's presidency to clear the way for a like-minded successor was seen by many liberals as a serious miscalculation that led to a dramatically more conservative court. Some conservative legal commentators addressed the possible ​political and actuarial implications if Democrats keep the Senate for years. "The Senate is ‌lost until 2032, so I hope Thomas and Alito got on their treadmills this morning," Ilya Shapiro, a senior fellow and director of constitutional studies at the Manhattan Institute, wrote in a ​social media post. Josh Hammer, a Newsweek podcaster and former clerk to Judge James Ho of the New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals, wrote in a social media post: "I ​hope Clarence Thomas and Sam Alito have historically great health insurance plans." (Reporting by John Kruzel; Editing by Will Dunham) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/conservative-us-supreme-court-justices-195338837.html

item.title: World leaders who sparred with Trump express relief mixed with caution at midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
LONDON (AP) — World leaders who have sparred with the "America first" President Donald Trump greeted the rout of his Republican Party in the U.S. midterm elections with a measure of relief Wednesday, allowing themselves to hope for a less combative U.S. foreign policy. But that hope was seasoned with the expectation that American voters' rebuke would not necessarily end the U.S. conflict with Iran or change Trump's policies on tariffs or his lukewarm-at-best support for Ukraine and America's European allies. Progressive politicians cast the results as part of a trend of liberal comebacks around the world, following recent defeats for populists on the right in Hungary , Brazil and Serbia . Spain's social democratic Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wrote on X that Americans had voted "Against hate. Against machismo. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites." "It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain," wrote Sánchez, who faces an election Nov. 29. Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said the majority of Americans had sent a clear message that "they have had enough of MAGA and now want a different course. Enough of polarization." Leaders are hopeful but wary British Prime Minister Andy Burnham expressed hope the election results would focus minds in Washington and other capitals on ending the Iran war, which has sent fuel prices soaring — a major source of frustration for voters. "The world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living," Burnham said during a visit to the Commonwealth summit in Antigua. "But I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved." That and "the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia. These are the things we have to focus on now." But others in Europe cautioned that, with Trump in power for two more years, there would be no quick change to American foreign policy, which has strained defense, economic and diplomatic alliances. The president has berated European leaders over everything from immigration to wind farms, roiled their economies with tariffs, threatened to pull the U.S. out of NATO and expressed a desire to take over Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of NATO ally Denmark. Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said that "independently of the election outcome, our security and prosperity in Austria and Europe must not depend on how people in Kansas or Iowa vote. That's why we are strengthening our own defense capability and our own competitiveness." Laurel Rapp, director of the U.S. and North America program at the Chatham House think tank, said there won't be "a 'we're back' moment in the U.S. relationship with Europe." "I don't expect this will significantly change the administration's approach to Europe," she said. "It's been a very transactional one, one that has deep skepticism about the value Europe can offer the U.S. in terms of a defense relationship." The United States' immediate neighbors reserved judgment on whether the Republican defeat would smooth rocky relations with Washington. "We must wait and see," said Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum. Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said it was unclear whether the election would strengthen Canada's hand in negotiations to end its bitter trade war . "Well, I guess we'll see in a few weeks," LeBlanc said. He noted that the new Congress would not take office until January and that Canada would continue negotiating with Trump's administration. But Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province has been battered by Trump's tariffs on automobiles and steel, celebrated the Democratic victory as a win for Canada and the world, saying it gave the country "a little more leverage." "I was doing cartwheels down the street," Ford said. Russia hopes Trump will stick to his current approach The Trump administration also has tried to pressure Ukraine to end a war that Russia started with its full-scale invasion in 2022. Ukraine accused Washington of delaying the delivery of vital interceptor missiles and reported that a temporary disruption to the Starlink and Starshield satellite internet service impeded its ability to defend against Russian attacks. Last month, even as he fired insults at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump waived sanctions on Russia even though Congress had overwhelmingly approved the measures as part of legislation aimed at supporting Ukraine. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that Russia hoped Trump "will continue his peacemaking efforts" regardless of the election outcome. A prominent German lawmaker urged Republicans to see the result in part as voters' verdict on Trump's "wrong foreign policy." Jürgen Hardt, a foreign policy spokesperson for the parliamentary group of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right bloc, told ARD television he hopes that Trump will "exercise more reason" on foreign affairs. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, who has been a target of Trump's baseless claims that his government discriminates against the country's white minority, said the Democrats taking control of both houses of Congress would "introduce a new era in world relations." But Rapp, from Chatham House, said that Congress will have an easier time constraining Trump domestically than in foreign policy. "On a lot of the foreign policy tools in his tool kit, Trump retains a lot of latitude to use them at his will," she said. ___ Gillies reported from Toronto. Associated Press writers Geir Moulson in Berlin, Suman Naishadham in Madrid, Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland, Gerald Imray in Cape Town, South Africa, and María Verza in Mexico City contributed to this story. item.title: Democrats' midterm victory was historic. These numbers show just how big it was.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Midterms tend to be backlash elections, and the president’s party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his performance in office. But not all midterms are created equal. On Tuesday, Democrats comprehensively routed their Republican rivals , regaining control of the U.S. House, U.S. Senate and statehouses across the country. Along the way, they shattered a series of decades-long Republican winning streaks and notched several historic firsts . So just how big was this year’s blue wave (or “ blue tsunami ”)? The full scale and scope of the Democratic Party’s seismic victory is still coming into focus as officials tally every last vote. But here are some key numbers to help you put it into perspective: Winning the House 26: the average number of House seats the president’s party has lost in midterm elections since World War II (pre-2026) 40+: the projected number of House seats that will flip to Democrats in 2026, once all the votes are counted About 255: the projected size of the new Democratic House majority — the largest since 2008, and possibly since 1992 6.8 percentage points: the Republican popular vote margin in their 1994 and 2010 House midterm victories 13 points: the projected Democratic popular vote margin in their 2026 House midterm victory 1974: the last time either party won their House popular vote by that much in a midterm election More than 100: the number of Democratic women who will serve simultaneously in the House — a historic first Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at an election night event on Nov. 4, 2026, in Detroit, as his wife Sarah Jukaku watches. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Flipping the Senate 4: the average number of Senate seats the president’s party has lost in midterm elections since World War II (pre-2026) 9: the number of Republican Senate seats that have either flipped to Democrats in 2026 (Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Texas) or could flip once all the votes are counted (Alaska, Mississippi) 55-56: the projected size of the new Democratic Senate majority — the largest since the early 2010s 2014: the last time a party — the Republicans — flipped 9 Senate seats in a midterm election 1958: the last time a party flipped more than 9 Senate seats in a midterm election 12 points: Trump’s average margin of victory in 2024 in the nine states where Democrats flipped or could still flip a Republican Senate seat this year 1986: The last midterm in which more than two Senate seats flipped in states where the president won by double-digit margins two years earlier At least 17: the number of senators from both parties who will be replaced in the chamber after the 2026 midterms — the largest turnover since 1980 70: the average age of this year’s departing senators At least 15: the number of senators from both parties who will be under 50 when they’re sworn into office in January 2027 — up from eight previously Georgia Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms, right, embraces her daughter, Lincoln, at an election night event on Nov. 3, 2026, in Atlanta. AP Photo/Brynn Anderson Closing the ‘governor gap’ 7: the number of Republican governorships that have either flipped to Democrats in 2026 (Iowa, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada, Texas) or could flip once all the votes are counted (Alaska, Kansas) As many as 31: the number of governorships that Democrats could control once all the votes are counted 2011: The last time Democrats controlled a majority of governorships About 75%: the percentage of Americans who will live in states with Democratic governors after the 2026 midterms How voters shifted 63%: the percentage of exit poll respondents who said item.title: A Mississippi Senate race nobody expected to be this close could end a 44-year streak
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
District Attorney and U.S. Senate candidate for Mississippi Scott Colom speaks as he gives an update on state of Senate race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Jackson, Mississippi, on Nov. 4, 2026. —Rogelio V. Solis—Getty Images As Democrats are celebrating a historic blue wave , eyes are on the Senate race in deep-red Mississippi, where the Democratic candidate led the Republican incumbent by a razor-thin margin of 1,138 votes as of Wednesday evening. The Associated Press has not yet called the race because it is so close, with Democratic challenger Scott Colom ahead by about 0.1%—he has so far earned 49% of the vote compared to Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith’s 48.9%, with 96% of votes counted. It’s a stunning nail-biter of a race that, in the weeks leading up to Election Day, polls had suggested would likely be won by the Republican incumbent by a narrow margin. “I can’t recall the last time it’s been this close for a statewide Senate contest—or a statewide election in general,” says Aaron Hitefield, an assistant professor of political science at Mississippi State University. “It’s unprecedented for [Mississippi] to be this competitive for Democrats particularly, certainly in the last 40 years.” Read More: What Democrats’ Midterm Gains Reveal About Trump’s Voter Coalition Political experts say it could take a few days before the outcome of the race becomes clear. If Colom, a district attorney, wins the race, it would be the first time that Mississippi voters have elected a Democrat to represent them in the U.S. Senate since 1982. A Democratic victory would also be a remarkable shift in a state that President Donald Trump won by a nearly 23-point margin just two years ago. Such an upset would cap off a string of staggering victories for Democrats, who have so far flipped seven seats in the upper chamber in this year’s midterm elections, including in other staunchly red states like Texas and South Carolina . Both candidates appeared to be optimistic that the election would ultimately go their way, though they also acknowledged that the race is still too close to call. Colom said in a statement early Wednesday morning, “I am confident we will ultimately flip this seat.” “The results are all trending in our direction,” Colom said in a speech to his supporters on Election Night. “The reality is, though, we’re not going to get the results tonight. I’m excited about our momentum, I’m excited about where we are.” Speaking to a crowd of her supporters on Election Night , Hyde-Smith said she was confident that she would hold her seat in the upper chamber. “We still don’t have all the votes in, so we’re not calling all of it tonight, but we’re in a very good lead and I assure you, I will continue to be your U.S. Senator,” she said . When asked about Hyde-Smith’s speech at a press conference on Wednesday, Colom replied , “Bless her heart.” When will we know who won the Mississippi Senate race? It is possible that the winner of the Senate contest may not be determined until the end of the week—or even next week. The state has five business days after Election Day to count affidavit ballots. An individual would turn in such a ballot, which is also called a provisional ballot, in a situation in which they believe they’re eligible and registered to vote but are unable to cast a standard ballot—for instance, if their name is not in their local polling place’s records. These votes are only counted once election workers verify the individual’s information. Mississippi also permits mail-in ballots that arrive within five days after Election Day, so long as they were postmarked by Election Day, to be counted. All this means that it’s possible the race may not be called until a week after Election Day, says Emily Ommundsen, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Mississippi. “Because of the razor-thin margins we currently see, I don’t expect any results to be called before then,” Ommundsen says. How did the Mississippi Senate race become such a tight contest? The tight race in Mississippi is one of many that illustrate the extremely challenging political environment Republicans have faced this year. Historically, the party in the White House loses seats in midterm elections, and that pressure on Republicans was compounded in this election cycle because of historically low approval for Trump driven in large part by the economy, as well as the war in Iran. Ommundsen says that, while ballots are still being counted, the result in Mississippi, so far, “is consistent with trends that we saw nationally.” “Nearly all counties that had a Senate election on the ballot moved towards the left compared to how they voted in 2024,” she says, though she notes that there are some exceptions. “Mississippi just happens to be one of those elections that was closer and perhaps more ripe for a flip.” Hitefield likens this year’s midterms to “a referendum on the President,” adding that “Democrats were turning out to oppose the President and to oppose the President’s policies.” But he cautions that the close contest in Mississippi is not necessarily a sign that the deep-red state is turning blue or even purple. It’s possible, he says, that Republican voters didn’t cast their ballots for a Democrat, and instead stayed home. “I wouldn’t necessarily read in, long story short, to Mississippi becoming a Georgia—you know, being a fully competitive every election state,” Hitefield says. “But I think it’s certainly moving toward a state that you shouldn’t sleep on when it comes to electoral competitiveness.” Hitefield also says that there’s a lot of “voter apathy” within the Republican party with regards to Hyde-Smith, and she hasn’t performed as well as Mississippi’s other Republican Senator, Roger Wicker, in past elections. Wicker won his re-election bid in 2024 by a more than 25-point margin . Hyde-Smith, meanwhile, won her re-election fight in 2020 by about 10 points . Hitefield adds that Hyde-Smith had some “gaffes” during the campaign, when she made some remarks about the rising cost of living that some voters felt were dismissive. For instance, when asked about soaring costs, including beef prices, during an interview with WLOX in February, Hyde-Smith applauded the passing of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill and went on to say, “It is on everybody’s mind. It is certainly me at my house. And you know, you have so many proteins to choose from. And all commodities go through peaks and valleys.” National polling ahead of Election Day indicated that an overwhelming majority of American voters felt that the economy was a crucial issue for them heading into this year’s midterms. Colom’s campaign jumped on Hyde-Smith’s remark, releasing an ad in which people objected to Hyde-Smith’s comment, including one who said in the video, “Pick another protein? Sh**, I’d rather pick another Senator instead.” The ad racked up more than 7.5 million views on Colom’s X account . Ommundsen points out that Hyde-Smith didn’t make many public campaign appearances in this year’s election cycle; one of the few appearances the Senator made was last week, when she gave very brief remarks at a rally the President held for her in Mississippi. Hitefield says Hyde-Smith didn’t “do the groundwork necessary to run a successful campaign” in this election cycle. “I think that it was a real mistake by her campaign, regardless of what the outcome looks like at the end of this,” Hitefield says. “Even if she does win, she didn’t do, really, what she needed to win with any sort of safety. I think that’s something [where] if she does win, she’ll need to think about, moving forward, how to strategize more effectively.” Colom, on the other hand, ran a “successful campaign” and generated “so much voter excitement,” Hitefield says—so much so that it stirred “this groundswell of hopes within the Democratic party that this seat could be flipped.” If Colom wins, he would also become the first Black Senator from Mississippi since the 19th century—the last time the state sent a Black lawmaker to the upper chamber was during Reconstruction in the aftermath of the Civil War. “It would be an unprecedented outcome when it comes to the history of Mississippi,” Hitefield says. This article originally appeared on Time at https://time.com/article/2026/11/05/mississippi-senate-race-2026-midterm-elections-colom-hyde-smith/

item.title: California's billionaire tax is losing despite a nationwide backlash against the rich
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
California's proposed billionaire tax appeared headed for defeat on Wednesday in one of the final verdicts from voters in an election week that saw a wave of anti-billionaire sentiment elsewhere. The latest results on Wednesday afternoon showed California's Proposition 40 down by over 11 percentage points, with 60% of votes counted but the race not yet formally called. The referendum would amend California's constitution and impose a one-time 5% tax on California residents and trusts with assets over $1 billion on Jan. 1, 2026. The revenue would primarily go toward healthcare, as well as food assistance and education. Some assets, such as real property and certain retirement accounts and pensions, were excluded. The measure was estimated to impact about 200 billionaires in the state. It faced fierce opposition from many in Big Tech and lost steam with voters as Election Day neared. People attend a rally against Proposition 40 on Oct. 5 in La Palma, Calif. (Eric Thayer/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) Eric Thayer via Getty Images Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) co-founder Sergey Brin was one of the measure's most vocal opponents. He contributed a reported $102 million to a political committee to fight the measure. Other billionaires made detailed plans in case it passed. Meta ( META ) CEO Mark Zuckerberg told his board, according to a New York Times report, that they needed to take steps to shield him from the tax or he would publicly list his home in Palo Alto for sale. The measure was also opposed by some Democrats, who argued it wouldn't work. Outgoing California Gov. Gavin Newsom emerged as an opponent, arguing that billionaires would both dodge the tax and leave the state. He cited a report from the California Legislative Analyst's Office that estimated the measure might temporarily boost state revenues but could be an overall drag on regular income taxes and "would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year." Across the country, voters in red and blue states delivered verdicts on wealth inequality and the influence of the ultrarich. In Texas, where Elon Musk spent more than $200 million to keep the state's Senate seat in Republican hands, voters flipped the seat for Democrats and made clear their unease over AI data centers . Tuesday's results also saw a series of wins by candidates who represent the Democratic Socialists of America , many of whom ran on explicitly anti-billionaire platforms. At least seven DSA members will take seats in Congress next year, as well as the mayors' offices of Los Angeles and Washington, D.C. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna are seen during a "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on Oct. 5 in Los Angeles. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) Justin Sullivan via Getty Images California voters were also weighing competing measures: Proposition 41 and Proposition 42 , which were introduced by opponents of Proposition 40 to prevent the wealth tax from taking effect. Proposition 42 would prohibit taxes on personal savings, assets, and retirement holdings. It was on track to pass based on the latest results. The wealth tax had support from progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Ro Khanna of California, who called the measure "the most important ballot initiative in America." Khanna on Tuesday night acknowledged the measure's fading prospects, saying in a press conference , "I'm proud of our efforts wherever we end up [and] I am going to be right there, first in line supporting this in the next election cycle if it doesn't pass this one." On Wednesday, Khanna wrote an op-ed for MS Now calling for a new federal tax on billionaires. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. This article originally appeared on Yahoo Finance at https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/californias-billionaire-tax-on-track-for-defeat-as-the-state-continues-to-count-votes-190840319.html

item.title: Trump Media falls to an all-time low as Democrats take back Congress
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump’s social media company and meme coin both plunged after Democrats won a decisive victory in the midterm elections, dinging the multibillion-dollar fortune of a president whose slew of new business ventures became a defining feature of his second term. Most Read from Bloomberg Morgan Stanley Offers $2.3 Billion Debt for Dell Family Deal Democrats Sweep to Control of Congress in Rebuke of Trump What the Democrats’ Sweep of Congress Means for Trump Democrat El-Sayed Wins Michigan Race in Boost to Progressives Democrats Clinch Huge Wins on Inflation Anger, Trump Fatigue Trump Media & Technology Group Corp., the parent company of social media platform Truth Social, touched an all-time low of $5.03 on Wednesday. $TRUMP, the virtual token that Trump introduced days before his second inauguration, slid more than 10% in the past 24 hours, according to data provider CoinMarketCap. The simultaneous drop in both assets — which trade heavily on retail speculation — signals investors may be anxious about the implications of the election for the businesses with links to the president, which are now expected to receive fresh congressional oversight. For months, Democrats have signaled their appetite to pursue investigations into the president and his family’s business interests if they prevail in either chamber, leaving any company connected to the first family as a potential target. “LAWYER UP,” Robert Garcia, the California Democrat in line to chair the House Oversight Committee, posted on social media as the results rolled in on Tuesday night. The businesses account for meaningful wealth for the first family. Trump’s stake in the social media company, which he holds through a trust controlled by his eldest son Donald Trump Jr, is worth about $600 million; the meme coin business accounts for about $83 million, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Trump shunned decades of norms for American presidents, drawing rebuke from the left for profiting from cryptocurrency ventures and business interests that bear his name while in office. When the New York Times asked the president earlier this year about conflicts of interest in his second term, he said, “I found out that nobody cared.” The White House has maintained that there are no conflicts of interests involving the president’s business ventures. Yet polling ahead of the midterms showed that government corruption, broadly, was a significant concern for voters. A Fox News poll found 60% of voters were extremely worried about government corruption, while a Gallup survey showed Americans’ perceptions of government corruption in the US hit their highest level in 20 years, with 89% of respondents calling it widespread. item.title: AI companies have reason to worry after Democrats won big in Texas
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A strong showing by Democrats in Texas swept Gina Hinojosa into office as the state's first Democratic governor since 1990 in a contest closely watched by Big Tech companies. Texas is considered a bellwether for government restrictions on AI data centers and was just one place where deep voter unease over the build-out was on display. Voters across the country passed a series of local ballot measures aimed at restricting construction in the years ahead. Hinojosa, Texas's first Latina governor, has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center construction in Texas, which accounts for more than 25% of planned US capacity by 2030. "I want to say something to the powerful people who have gotten very comfortable running this state," she told supporters in her victory speech . "The voters have delivered a mandate for change, and it is change they will get." Her victory was one of a series of wins for Democrats in Texas. The party is also on track to take control of the Texas House , which would give Hinojosa more power to follow through on restrictions even as the state Senate appears set to remain under Republican control. Democratic gubernatorial candidate State Rep. Gina Hinojosa speaks to her election night watch party on Nov. 3 in Austin, Texas. (Joel Angel Juarez/Getty Images) Joel Angel Juarez via Getty Images "We view the Texas gubernatorial race as particularly important for the next leg of the AI trade," wrote Raymond James's Ed Mills in a pre-election note saying that a strong Democratic showing there "could signal a broader electoral wave while increasing concerns about data center moratoriums and more restrictive AI regulation in the nation's largest planned data center development." Bank of America called the race "one of the highest impact elections for the entire utility sector." A race that 'could make a real difference' Hinojosa made opposition to data center construction a central part of her campaign, charging in one ad that Gov. Greg Abbott "works for" Elon Musk. She staked out plans for a moratorium on new data center construction, stricter regulations on water and power usage, and an end to tax breaks. Abbott was seeking his fourth term as governor and said last year he wanted Texas to be the "epicenter of AI development." More recently, he announced a moratorium of his own and said he would support more stringent requirements on power and water usage. Hinojosa immediately charged that Abbott's new proposals amounted to an "election year pause." Tobin Marcus of Wolfe Research said Texas "is the one state with enough scale and enough difference between the candidates that it could make a real difference." Texas Gov. Greg Abbott speaks to the media after casting his ballot on Oct. 19 in Del Valle, Texas. (Sergio Flores/Getty Images) Sergio Flores via Getty Images Voters who feel 'AI will do more to hurt society' The race reflected a national mood that has turned sharply against data centers in recent months. NBC exit polls on Tuesday showed that 57% of voters felt "AI will do more to hurt society" compared to just 24% who said it would help. A UMass Amherst Poll in September also found nearly two-thirds of Americans oppose AI data center construction in their communities, with just 11% of voters welcoming them On Tuesday, voters weighed in on data center ballot measures in contests spanning 13 states, from Arkansas to Wisconsin. One tracker counted 28 measures before voters to limit data centers. On Wednesday morning, with votes still being counted, virtually every one was on track to pass. In Ohio alone, voters in at least 14 municipalities passed bans or other restrictions . Ohio Democratic Senate candidate former Sen. Sherrod Brown speaks during a midterm election night watch party in Columbus on Nov. 3. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images) Michael M. Santiago via Getty Images In the Ohio Senate race, voters elected Democrat Sherrod Brown, who, like Hinojosa, made opposition to data center construction a key part of his campaign message. "I do not work for the utility companies, I do not work for data centers," Brown said as he declared victory on Tuesday night . Even Elon Musk seemed to acknowledge the dour public sentiment toward data centers. He quipped in a post early Wednesday as the results became clear, "data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now." This story has been updated. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.
